$$

$$

e-10992.problem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14081590/assets/28a22a5f860f02e42abc699e9807de885cc01b572c23ac0d4f909fe281042e08.png)
e-10992.worked_solution:
Notice that the $1$st column contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $1$st column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 5 & 5 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 13 & 19 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 0 \\ 13 & 19 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 0 \\ 13 & 19 & -3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 0 \\ 13 & 19 & -3\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot 2\cdot (-3)=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\det(A) = 2 \cdot (-6) = -12.
$$

e-10998.knowledge_point: Computing the Volume of an N-Dimensional Parallelepiped
e-10998.problem:
Calculate the volume of the $4$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the vectors

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14081590/assets/c185678d20cabf2a302c0101876f9fb67fd35cf682f547f62a9eeb99fd97946f.png)
e-10998.worked_solution:
First, let's construct the matrix $M,$ whose columns are the coordinates of our vectors $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ $\mathbf{c},$ and  $\mathbf{d}{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14081590/assets/923b0fb4f65d4de6538658d49e32fb3256fd374b1cc94dd62256f9e966c72d24.png)

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by these vectors equals the absolute value of the determinant of $M{:}$

$$
V = | \det(M) |
$$

Notice that the $2$nd row of the determinant contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & -4 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the $2$nd row of the $3 \times 3$ determinant contains two zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =-3|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot 1\cdot (-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3(15+4) \\  & =-57.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume is

$$
V = | \det(M) | = |-57| = 57.
$$

e-10993.knowledge_point: Calculating an Expression Involving Given Determinants and Matrix Types
e-10993.problem:
Given that $\det(A)=4,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $\textrm{det}(A^T)=16$

- $3\textrm{det}(A^T)=12$

- $\textrm{det}(A^T)+\textrm{det}(I)=17$
e-10993.worked_solution:
From the properties of determinants, we know that 

$$
\textrm{det}(A^T)=\textrm{det}(A)=4
$$

and

$$
\textrm{det}(I)=1.
$$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Rather, 

$$
\textrm{det}(A^T)=4 \neq 16.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
3\textrm{det}(A^T)= 3 \cdot 4 = 12.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\textrm{det}(A^T)+\textrm{det}(I)= 4 + 1 = 5 \neq 17.
$$

In conclusion, the correct answer is "II only".

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Find the determinant of the matrix 
$B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 1 & 19 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the $3$rd column contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $3$rd column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 1 & 19 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =3\cdot 1\cdot (-3)=-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
det(B)=-9.
$$

content.problem:
Find the determinant of the matrix 
$G=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 13 & 6 & 7 & -2\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the $4$th column contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $4$th column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(G) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 13 & 6 & 7 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-1)^{4+4}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}| & =(-2)\cdot (1\cdot 2\cdot (-1))=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
det(G)=4.
$$

$$

$$
